paragraphs: ATLAS evaluates language models by choosing questions adaptively rather than administering an entire fixed benchmark. Its starting point is that questions differ in difficulty and in how effectively they distinguish models. An average accuracy score treats every answer equally, potentially spending evaluation effort on questions that add little information about a particular model.

The framework uses Item Response Theory to estimate model ability. It selects questions using Fisher information, a measure of how informative an observation is for estimating that ability. The reported results show reductions of up to 90% in required items while retaining measurement precision. On HellaSwag, 41 questions approximate ability estimates from a 5,600-item bank with a mean absolute error of 0.157.

Across five benchmarks, accuracies reconstructed from ability estimates closely track raw accuracy, suggesting that the shorter evaluations retain broad performance patterns. They also distinguish models that accuracy places together: among more than 3,000 models, 23–31% move over ten ranking positions. These changes reflect a different measurement of performance, incorporating which questions models answer successfully.
icml-2026-adaptive-testing-for-llm-evalu.tldr: ATLAS adaptively selects informative benchmark questions to estimate LLM ability with fewer evaluations and distinguish models with similar accuracy.

paragraphs: Hypergraphs represent relationships involving groups of nodes, making them richer than graphs restricted to pairwise connections. Training neural networks on large hypergraphs can be expensive. Hypergraph condensation addresses this by creating a small synthetic hypergraph that retains useful training information. This paper targets how that synthetic data is constructed and refined.

The authors identify a coordination problem in existing methods: a structure generator is trained separately and then remains disconnected from feature refinement. As synthetic node features change, their associated relationships can become poorly matched. AHGCDD begins with Heat Kernel PageRank initialization to incorporate structural information into node features, then uses anchors to synthesize hyperedges while jointly optimizing features and structure.

A dual-level discrimination objective guides condensation without the redundant hypergraph-network training associated with trajectory-based refinement. The abstract describes this objective as theoretically grounded and reports experiments showing improved effectiveness and efficiency. The central contribution is therefore coordinated compression: the compact hypergraph's features and group relationships develop together, while a different refinement objective reduces the work needed to preserve downstream usefulness.
icml-2026-anchor-guided-hypergraph-conde.tldr: AHGCDD condenses hypergraphs by jointly refining synthetic features and relationships while reducing repeated neural-network training.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding speeds up language generation by having a fast model propose tokens that a larger target model checks together. Under sampling, however, the usual lossless verification rule can reject drafts even when accepting them would introduce little distributional risk. This reduces the amount of useful text produced during each verification cycle.

ARC-Decode adds a training-free acceptance mechanism without requiring extra forward passes. It first filters proposals using confidence, then applies a risk-controlled criterion based on Jensen–Shannon divergence, which measures differences between probability distributions. An analytic upper bound on potential distributional deviation supports the relaxed acceptance decision. This makes the risk associated with accepting a draft part of the verification procedure.

Integrated into EAGLE-3, the method accepts longer sequences per cycle and reduces verification computation. The experiments report up to 1.6 times end-to-end speedup over EAGLE-3 under sampling, with negligible quality change across the evaluated benchmarks. The result supports risk-bounded relaxation as a practical acceleration strategy; the stated mechanism controls potential distributional deviation rather than establishing unconditional equivalence for every relaxed acceptance.
icml-2026-arc-decode-accelerated-decodin.tldr: ARC-Decode accelerates speculative sampling by relaxing draft acceptance under a distributional-risk bound, achieving up to 1.6 times speedup over EAGLE-3.

paragraphs: Language-model reinforcement learning needs to control how much a policy changes during an update. PPO uses fixed clipping bounds as an efficient approximation to a trust region. This paper identifies a drawback: for actions that already have low probability, those bounds severely restrict upward movement, even when the actions have high estimated advantage.

BandPO replaces fixed clipping with probability-aware intervals. Its Band operator translates trust regions defined through f-divergences into bounds tailored to action probabilities. This connects the intended restriction on policy change to the clipping mechanism used during optimization. The mapping is formulated as a convex optimization problem, supporting a globally optimal numerical solution, with closed-form solutions available for particular divergences.

The theoretical analysis establishes that Band addresses the identified exploration bottleneck. Experiments across different models and datasets report consistent improvements over canonical clipping and Clip-Higher, together with reduced entropy collapse. Entropy collapse means the policy's choices rapidly become less diverse. The findings suggest that adapting update bounds to action probability can preserve exploration while retaining proximal constraints on learning.
icml-2026-bandpo-bridging-trust-regions-.tldr: BandPO derives probability-aware clipping bounds from trust regions to improve LLM reinforcement learning and mitigate entropy collapse.

paragraphs: Different machine-learning models can develop similar internal representations, even when they process different kinds of input. Much existing work measures or characterizes that alignment. This paper instead investigates two possible contributors: overlap in the data models encounter and overlap in the tasks they learn to perform.

The authors examine these factors through experiments spanning model sizes and modalities, from small classifiers to large language models. Across many settings, greater dataset overlap and greater task overlap are associated with greater representational similarity. The pattern is clearer for vision and language classification, while language-generation experiments show weaker trends. The evidence therefore varies with the learning setting rather than supporting a uniform relationship across every model.

The paper also examines a practical consequence in vision models. Greater representational similarity is associated with increased vulnerability to adversarial attacks that transfer between models. This connects internal alignment to shared failure behavior: similarity can matter beyond how representations look under a comparison metric. The reported relationships motivate considering both training overlap and attack transfer when interpreting model similarity.
icml-2026-causes-and-consequences-of-rep.tldr: Dataset and task overlap are associated with greater model-representation similarity, which also correlates with adversarial attack transfer in vision models.

paragraphs: Language models can produce formal proofs, but strong results often require many attempts or very long contexts. This paper addresses that computational burden by using the structure of compiler feedback. Although attempted proofs can vary enormously, their failures map into a smaller collection of structured error types.

The proposed learning-to-refine framework uses that compressed feedback to guide proof exploration. It performs tree search in which local corrections are conditioned on explicit verifier responses. This allows the search to focus on repairing identified errors without accumulating a long history of entire proof attempts. Compiler output therefore serves as a concise signal for deciding how a candidate proof should change.

Evaluations report improvements to base provers across different model scales. On PutnamBench, the method achieves the strongest publicly reported performance among approximately 8-billion- and 32-billion-parameter models under comparable test-time budgets. That qualification matters: the result compares particular model-size groups and computational budgets. The broader contribution is a way to make verifier-guided reasoning more efficient by organizing search around structured failures and local refinement.
icml-2026-compile-to-compress-boosting-f.tldr: A verifier-guided refinement framework uses structured compiler errors to improve formal proof search without retaining long histories of attempts.

paragraphs: This paper studies episodic decision-making in finite-state, finite-action environments whose transition rules are known. It develops algorithms with regret guarantees that adapt to the observed problem's difficulty. Regret measures the accumulated disadvantage relative to a comparison policy, so a more adaptive bound can distinguish easier learning sequences from worst-case ones.

The analysis covers both adversarial and stochastic regimes. For adversarial settings, it introduces several data-dependent complexity measures, including second-order and path-length quantities. For stochastic settings, the guarantees depend on variance. Both global-optimization and policy-optimization algorithms use optimistic follow-the-regularized-leader with log-barrier regularization. A new optimistic Q-function estimator enables the policy-optimization approach to obtain similar adaptivity, with an additional episode-horizon factor.

For global optimization, the stochastic results include a variance-aware bound independent of gaps and a gap-dependent bound growing only polylogarithmically with episode count. Matching lower-bound analysis shows that its guarantees are nearly optimal in terms of the studied complexity measures. These are theoretical results under known transitions, explaining how achievable regret can depend on data structure and variability.
icml-2026-data-and-variance-dependent-re.tldr: For tabular MDPs with known transitions, new algorithms achieve regret bounds that adapt to data complexity and stochastic variance.

paragraphs: DECO addresses how a two-arm robot should combine visual input, information about its own configuration, and touch. These signals describe different aspects of manipulation. The model gives them specialized conditioning pathways within a diffusion transformer, allowing their contributions to be integrated in a structured and controllable way.

A lightweight adapter provides a parameter-efficient route for adding signals, including tactile information. The authors also release DECO-50, containing 50 hours and more than five million frames of tactile-enabled manipulation data collected by teleoperating real dual-arm robots. They train DECO on this dataset and evaluate it through more than 2,000 real-world robot rollouts.

DECO reports the best performance across the evaluated tasks, with 72.25% average success and a reported 21% improvement over the baseline. The tactile adapter contributes an additional reported 10.25% average success rate across tasks and a 20% gain on complex tasks involving substantial contact, while tuning fewer than 10% of model parameters. These findings support both separating sensory pathways and adding touch through a small adaptable component.
icml-2026-deco-decoupled-multimodal-diff.tldr: DECO separates sensory conditioning for two-arm manipulation and uses a lightweight tactile adapter to improve real-world task success.

paragraphs: Visual autoregressive models generate images through successive scale predictions. The later, larger-scale steps can require sharply more computation, making them an important target for acceleration. FasterVAR studies how the roles of generation stages differ so that computational reductions can reflect their importance to the resulting image.

The authors find that early steps are critical for semantic and structural consistency, while later steps mainly refine detail. Their framework preserves the early stages and prunes or approximates selected late-stage computations. It uses the limited semantic relevance and low-rank properties of those computations to identify opportunities for savings. The approach is designed to plug into existing models without additional training.

Experiments report speedups of up to 3.4 times with almost no performance loss, consistently exceeding the evaluated acceleration baselines. This supports a stage-aware approach to efficiency: computation receives different treatment depending on its role in generation. The stated finding concerns preserving early image organization while simplifying later refinement, providing a more systematic basis for acceleration than manually choosing steps to modify.
icml-2026-fastervar-plug-and-play-accele.tldr: FasterVAR preserves early image-generation stages and simplifies later computations, achieving up to 3.4 times speedup without additional training.

paragraphs: Federated graph learning combines learning across clients that hold local graph data. Incorrect node labels can damage the shared model, and noise-handling methods developed for images may overlook information provided by graph relationships. FedRGL uses both local structure and the globally aggregated model to identify questionable supervision.

Its class-aware dual-consistency filtering compares these two perspectives using thresholds that change by class. The filtering module can also be inserted into other subgraph federated-learning frameworks. Rather than simply discarding flagged nodes, FedRGL uses graph-contrastive augmentations to assign high-confidence replacement labels. On the server, average predictive entropy on unlabeled nodes estimates model quality and guides adaptive aggregation.

Experiments on real-world graphs vary noise rates, noise types, and the number of clients. The reported results show average accuracy improvements of 5–8%, with gains reaching 30% against the weakest baselines under noisy conditions. The method's contribution spans the learning process: detect unreliable labels using graph-aware evidence, recover useful supervision from affected nodes, and adjust how client models contribute to the shared result.
icml-2026-fedrgl-robust-federated-graph-.tldr: FedRGL improves federated graph learning under label noise through graph-aware filtering, confident relabeling, and adaptive server aggregation.

paragraphs: DynaDiff addresses dynamics predictors whose accuracy deteriorates when the environment changes. Repeated fine-tuning can be costly when hardware or new observations are limited. The proposed framework instead learns to generate predictor weights directly, using observations of the new environment to condition a diffusion model.

The method represents expert-model weights as graphs and uses multi-head attention to capture relationships within those weights. A functional loss encourages generated predictors to match expert models in physical behavior, connecting weight generation to what the resulting model actually predicts. A dynamics-informed prompter extracts physical and spectral features from observation sequences and supplies this information to the generator.

The experiments report a 10.78% average prediction-accuracy improvement over competitive baselines. Deployment efficiency comes from preparing a collection of expert predictors beforehand, moving fine-tuning overhead into a one-time offline cost. The approach therefore depends on this prior preparation: its contribution is to reuse expert-model knowledge through conditional weight generation, making adaptation to new environments less dependent on repeated optimization at deployment.
icml-2026-generative-adaptation-of-dynam.tldr: DynaDiff generates dynamics-model weights from environmental observations, using offline expert preparation to improve adaptation accuracy and deployment efficiency.

paragraphs: HeraSys targets serving environments where many users run agentic language-model workflows concurrently. Each workflow contains multiple computational steps, and optimizing those steps within one workflow can miss shared work across workflows. The system treats concurrent execution as an opportunity for both reuse and coordinated scheduling.

It merges and reuses structurally matching workflow nodes to remove redundant computation. A load-aware scheduler considers priorities both within and across queries when deciding execution order. Resource skewing, adaptive batching, and pipeline decomposition then work together to manage execution. These mechanisms aim to keep average response times low while also reducing unusually slow completions.

The experiments report P99 latency reductions by a factor of up to 2.17 and throughput increases of up to 1.85 times under strict latency guarantees. P99 latency describes the slow end of the response-time distribution, so that improvement concerns requests poorly represented by the average alone. The results support optimizing whole concurrent workflows together, with shared computation and scheduling contributing to end-to-end serving performance.
icml-2026-herasys-collaborative-serving-.tldr: HeraSys combines cross-workflow computation reuse and coordinated scheduling to improve LLM serving throughput and tail latency.

paragraphs: LLM4PH tests whether language models can reason about graph structure as it changes across scales. Conventional graph benchmarks often emphasize local relationships or a single static view. The proposed benchmark instead uses persistent homology, a mathematical framework for tracking how structural features evolve and persist.

The authors divide the persistent-homology pipeline into interpretable reasoning tasks on synthetic and real-world graphs. This decomposition allows evaluation of individual parts of the reasoning process. They also assemble a compositional pipeline to measure end-to-end performance, examine prompt encodings and transfer across tasks, and explore the effects of post-training.

The results show that most evaluated models struggle with structural transitions and persistence. This identifies a challenge beyond recognizing graph elements: models must relate discrete structures to an abstraction that follows changes across multiple scales. By testing both components and their composition, LLM4PH provides a more detailed picture of that capability. The benchmark offers evidence relevant to structure-aware scientific reasoning without establishing that current models reliably perform the full process.
icml-2026-large-language-models-as-topol.tldr: LLM4PH benchmarks multiscale graph reasoning through persistent homology and finds that most models struggle with structural change and persistence.

paragraphs: Constrained multi-objective reinforcement learning seeks several useful trade-offs that also satisfy feasibility requirements. CoPro addresses difficulties caused by changing objective scales, nearly tied candidates, and groups containing few feasible options. Its goal is progress along the feasible Pareto front, where improving one objective entails sacrificing another.

The method alternates between two projections. First, it computes nonnegative weights over a sampled group through a KL-regularized optimization with moment constraints. These weights favor feasible progress, retain feasible anchors, and suppress ambiguous near-ties. The solution has an exponential-family form. Its guarantee is conditional: feasible anchors receive strictly positive probability whenever feasible candidates occur in the sampled group.

Second, weighted maximum likelihood moves the policy toward that distribution, with a trust-region regularizer controlling the update. This derives a direction from comparisons without requiring manually designed reward shaping. Experiments on language-model tool use and analog circuit design report better feasible-front quality and robustness. The contribution is a structured way to translate group comparisons into policy updates while preserving available feasible reference points.
icml-2026-learning-from-comparison-const.tldr: CoPro converts candidate comparisons into constrained policy updates that improve feasible multi-objective trade-offs while preserving available feasibility anchors.

paragraphs: MIMOMamba extends the mathematical framework connecting state-space sequence models with attention-like computation. Existing state space duality formulations use a restrictive scalar-identity condition to preserve commutativity, meaning certain state-transition operations can exchange order. That condition limits interactions between different dimensions of the model's internal state.

The paper generalizes the framework from single-input, single-output systems to multiple inputs and outputs. It parameterizes transitions with matrix polynomials, maintaining the commutativity needed for the duality while allowing richer cross-dimensional dynamics. The same construction gives transitions a shared algebraic structure, reducing redundant parameters. This makes the mathematical extension relevant to both expressiveness and model size.

Building on that foundation, the authors introduce a multi-head state-space architecture that retains linear-time training. On a sequence-modeling benchmark, it performs comparably to or better than standard Transformers while using substantially fewer parameters. The empirical finding is specific to that evaluation, while the broader technical contribution is a structured route to richer state interactions without giving up the framework's efficient training behavior.
icml-2026-mimomamba-from-scalar-duality-.tldr: MIMOMamba uses matrix-polynomial state transitions to enable richer cross-dimensional interactions while retaining linear-time training and reducing parameter redundancy.

paragraphs: UniEFS investigates reconstructing whole-brain fMRI activity from EEG recordings. fMRI provides detailed spatial measurements but requires costly, restrictive acquisition, while EEG offers more accessible scalp recordings. The paper addresses a limitation of earlier translation methods: separate region-specific models and limited accommodation of differences between people and datasets.

The proposed system uses one model for full-brain reconstruction. A pretrained fMRI decoder contributes learned spatial structure, while condition-aware prompt tokens represent subject and experimental metadata. These prompts allow demographic and physiological context to influence synthesis. The design brings spatial knowledge and contextual information into the same translation model rather than treating all recordings as interchangeable.

Evaluation on eyes-closed resting-state data reports reliable reconstruction of whole-brain activity over time. The abstract also identifies potential for zero-shot generalization to task-based fMRI and clinical populations, which remains a qualified claim rather than established universal performance. The main result supports context-aware, unified synthesis in the evaluated resting-state setting, with broader applications presented as possible extensions.
icml-2026-mind-the-state-towards-unified.tldr: UniEFS combines pretrained fMRI spatial knowledge with contextual prompts to reconstruct whole-brain activity from EEG in a unified model.

paragraphs: Nevo-CRL addresses continual reinforcement learning: acquiring new skills while retaining and reusing earlier ones. It keeps a single policy network with fixed capacity and changes which neurons participate in each task. This makes connectivity selection, alongside neuron parameters, a central part of learning.

For a new task, the method creates a population of masks that selectively activate hidden-layer outputs, producing different candidate policies. Importance-guided crossover updates these masks during training. After completing the task, it stores the best mask and freezes the neurons that mask activates to protect the acquired skill. For later tasks, semantic similarity guides reuse of neurons associated with prior skills.

Additional neurons are allocated for task-specific adaptation, and low-activity connections are pruned to recycle neurons and improve utilization. These mechanisms combine protection, transfer, and resource reuse within a fixed-size network. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated continual reinforcement-learning methods. The contribution is a coordinated allocation strategy: preserve useful established components while searching for connections that support new tasks.
icml-2026-neuro-evolutionary-continual-r.tldr: Nevo-CRL evolves task-specific neuron masks within a fixed-capacity policy network to preserve skills, transfer knowledge, and recycle resources.

paragraphs: OpenSage is an agent development kit designed to let language models construct more of their own working organization. The paper argues that agent performance depends heavily on how agents, tools, and memory are arranged, yet existing kits either provide insufficient support or leave these decisions to human developers.

The system allows agents to create and manage sub-agents and toolkits, including generating their own topology and toolsets. It pairs this functionality with hierarchical, graph-based memory intended to support efficient, structured information management. A specialized toolkit supports software-engineering tasks. These components give the model facilities for both organizing work and retaining information within the resulting agent system.

Experiments across three benchmarks and several backbone models report advantages over existing agent development kits. Ablation studies examine the effectiveness of individual design components. The findings support the usefulness of the combined development infrastructure in those evaluations. The authors' broader ambition is a shift toward AI-directed agent construction, with automatic organization and tool creation taking on responsibilities commonly handled manually.
icml-2026-opensage-self-programming-agen.tldr: OpenSage lets LLM agents generate and manage their own sub-agents and tools, supported by structured graph-based memory.

paragraphs: Parametric Prior Mapping addresses forecasting multiple related time series whose behavior changes over time. Probabilistic forecasting must describe both expected outcomes and uncertainty. The paper starts from a tension: parametric methods offer useful structure and efficiency, while flexible generative models can demand substantial data and computation to capture temporal relationships.

PPM combines these approaches by using a parametric estimator to construct a dynamic, adaptive prior. A learnable mapping then uses that prior to guide a richer predictive distribution. The parametric component supplies structural guidance, while the generative component provides flexibility beyond the initial estimate. A hybrid training objective supports the combined forecasting process.

The authors report precise forecasts with well-calibrated uncertainty and stronger performance than existing baselines on non-stationary data. They also report a better balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. These findings suggest that adaptive structural priors can help a flexible model handle changing temporal behavior efficiently. The contribution lies in making the prior an active, learned bridge between a compact estimator and a more expressive predictive distribution.
icml-2026-parametric-prior-mapping-frame.tldr: PPM guides generative time-series forecasting with adaptive parametric priors to combine expressive predictions, calibrated uncertainty, and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: When language models analyze database rows, processing the input prompt can be a major cost. Relational tables often repeat attribute values, but ordinary row-by-row layouts may place those values where they cannot form reusable prompt prefixes. This leaves potential savings from prefix key-value caching unrealized.

The paper connects prompt-prefix reuse to the shape of a radix tree induced by the table's data distribution. A radix tree groups shared beginnings, making the relationship between layout and reuse explicit. Based on this connection, SOLO uses a greedy tree-shaping algorithm to choose row and column orderings that increase shared prefixes. The approach uses relational structure to guide planning.

Under a fixed prefix-cache budget, the reported experiments show prefill-throughput improvements of up to 90.3%. Planning overhead falls by a factor of up to 242 compared with the evaluated state-of-the-art baselines. These results distinguish two benefits: less work during prompt processing and cheaper selection of the layout itself. The contribution is a practical way to make repeated table content reusable by the model-serving cache.
icml-2026-prefix-cache-aware-data-reorde.tldr: SOLO reorders database rows and columns to expose shared prompt prefixes, improving cache reuse and reducing layout-planning overhead.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a model using inputs encountered during inference, helping it handle data that differs from training. Those updates also make model parameters depend on previous test inputs, creating a privacy concern. This paper studies how to control that dependence while preserving the benefits of adaptation.

The authors convert Tent, EATA, SAR, DeYO, and COME into differentially private variants. Every update clips each sample's gradient and adds Gaussian noise. Clipping limits how strongly an individual input can affect an update, while the noise is part of the privacy mechanism. Applying these changes across several methods examines private adaptation as a broader approach rather than a modification to only one algorithm.

On ImageNet-C, the resulting methods provide privacy with a small accuracy cost and modest computational overhead. In the low-privacy regime, clipping can additionally improve accuracy and stability during continual adaptation. That improvement is conditional on the reported regime, not a claim that stronger privacy always improves accuracy. The findings also identify per-sample clipping as a useful stabilizing component in its own right.
icml-2026-private-and-stable-test-time-a.tldr: Differentially private test-time updates protect inference data with small reported accuracy costs, while clipping can also stabilize continual adaptation.

paragraphs: ReSeek addresses search agents that follow an unhelpful reasoning path and fail to recover. Reinforcement-learning methods with sparse or rule-based rewards may provide insufficient guidance during a multi-step search. The proposed framework makes reassessment an explicit action the agent can take within the same episode.

Through a special JUDGE action, the agent evaluates the information it has gathered and replans its search strategy. Training uses a dense process reward with two components: correctness rewards factual retrieval, while utility rewards information useful for the particular query. This distinction matters because information can be factually correct without helping resolve the user's question.

The authors also introduce FictionalHot, described as a contamination-free benchmark requiring complex reasoning, to address contamination risks in existing datasets. Experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in task success and path faithfulness. The central contribution combines a mechanism for recovery with feedback that teaches when search evidence is both accurate and useful, supporting correction during reasoning rather than only evaluation of the final outcome.
icml-2026-reseek-a-self-correcting-frame.tldr: ReSeek trains search agents to reassess and repair their search paths using a JUDGE action and rewards for factual correctness and usefulness.

paragraphs: Diffusion and flow policies offer expressive action distributions, but online reinforcement learning lacks direct samples from the desired Boltzmann distribution defined by the Q-function. Existing diffusion-policy methods address this using either weighted noise averages or weighted Q-gradient averages. Reverse flow matching explains how these apparently different training targets fit together.

RFM views training as estimating a posterior mean given an intermediate noisy sample. It uses Langevin Stein operators to construct zero-mean control variates: adjustments that preserve an estimator's expectation. This produces a broader family of estimators containing both existing noise-expectation and gradient-expectation approaches as special cases.

The framework extends Boltzmann-targeting training to flow policies and provides a principled way to combine Q-values with Q-gradients. The authors report that this combination improves training efficiency and stability. They instantiate the approach with a flow policy and show improved continuous-control performance relative to diffusion-policy baselines. Its contribution is both conceptual and practical: a common estimation framework clarifies existing objectives and supports a new way to train expressive policies without direct target samples.
icml-2026-reverse-flow-matching-a-unifie.tldr: Reverse flow matching unifies diffusion-policy training objectives and combines Q-value and Q-gradient information to train flow policies without direct target samples.

paragraphs: Scene text editing changes words inside an image while retaining the surrounding appearance. The paper argues that methods relying only on background information lose useful style cues in the original text itself. It also identifies pretrained glyph encoders as a restriction on which text can be edited.

The proposed method builds style and glyph prompts directly from the original image, without separate encoders for either purpose. These prompts allow the diffusion transformer to use visual information from the text being replaced. Training proceeds in two stages: large-scale self-supervised learning followed by refinement on a small collection of paired images. The approach uses FLUX-Fill's in-context learning capability to support open-vocabulary editing.

Experiments across multiple languages report state-of-the-art results for both text accuracy and style consistency. These are complementary requirements: an edit must produce the intended characters while fitting the original image's visual treatment. The contribution is to preserve and reuse the target region's own stylistic evidence, giving the editing model more relevant guidance than background appearance alone.
icml-2026-self-prompting-diffusion-trans.tldr: A self-prompting diffusion transformer reuses image-derived style and glyph cues for accurate, style-consistent scene text editing across languages.

paragraphs: Optimization methods can favor particular solutions even without explicitly requesting them, a phenomenon called implicit bias. This paper studies that preference for mini-batch stochastic steepest descent in multiclass classification. It covers geometries induced by entry-wise and Schatten-p norms, connecting the analysis to methods such as SignSGD and Muon.

The results distinguish the effects of batch size, momentum, and variance reduction. Without momentum, worst-case convergence and successful classification can only be guaranteed with full-batch gradients in the studied setting. Momentum allows small batches to approach an approximate maximum-margin solution through a batch–momentum trade-off, although convergence becomes slower. The authors provide explicit, dimension-free convergence rates.

Variance reduction can recover the exact full-batch implicit bias at any batch size, again at a slower rate. A concrete example also shows that batch-size-one updates without momentum converge to a fundamentally different bias. This demonstrates a possible divergence from full-batch behavior, rather than universal failure of stochastic learning. Together, the results explain which mechanisms can align stochastic solution preferences with their full-batch counterparts.
icml-2026-the-implicit-bias-of-steepest-.tldr: The analysis shows how momentum and variance reduction can recover approximate or exact full-batch solution preferences in stochastic steepest descent.
